content.text: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
Understand what the gradient of a line measures
Calculate the gradient of a line from a graph
Use the gradient formula $m = \frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}$
Recognise positive, negative, zero, and undefined gradients
Interpret the gradient in real-world contexts

) of a line tells us how steep it is and in which direction it slopes. In everyday life, gradients describe the steepness of hills (a road sign showing a 10% gradient), the rate at which temperature changes, or how quickly costs increase. In mathematics, the gradient is a precise numerical measure of how much $y$ changes for every unit increase in $x$.
of a straight line is the rate at which $y$ increases as $x$ increases. It is the ratio of the vertical change to the horizontal change between any two points on the line.
$$m = \frac{\text{change in } y}{\text{change in } x} = \frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}} = \frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}$$
where $(x_1, y_1)$ and $(x_2, y_2)$ are any two points on the line.
Line slopes upward from left to right
Line slopes downward from left to right
A larger positive gradient means a steeper upward slope. A more negative gradient means a steeper downward slope.

Find the gradient of the line passing through $(2, 3)$ and $(6, 11)$.
The gradient is $2$. This means for every 1 unit increase in $x$, $y$ increases by 2.
Find the gradient of the line passing through $(1, 8)$ and $(5, 2)$.
The gradient is $-\frac{3}{2}$. The negative sign tells us the line slopes downward.
Find the gradient of the line passing through $(-3, -4)$ and $(1, 8)$.
Be very careful with subtracting negative numbers: $8 - (-4) = 8 + 4 = 12$.
